rationale: Self-reported inspiratory stridor is not a symptom of adult laryngitis; stridor is an expedited-laryngoscopy indicator in the AAO-HNS 2018 dysphonia guideline (KAS 3), so the airway must be visualised before the label stands.

Hospitalisation for asthma within the past year is a SIGN 158 section 9.1 marker of near-fatal asthma risk; cough and wheeze after a cold in that patient is an exacerbation, and the bronchitis label omits the systemic steroid and peak-flow severity assessment it needs.

Palpitations with light-headedness on caffeine, energy drinks and decongestants in a 19-year-old: the ESC 2018 syncope initial evaluation (history, orthostatic blood pressure, 12-lead ECG) is an office check, and no chest pain or high-risk marker mandates troponin or imaging.

Weight loss, back-radiating epigastric pain, nausea and diarrhoea in chronic pancreatitis with a family history of pancreatic cancer need pancreatic imaging: NICE NG104 1.3.10 treats pain and weight loss as markers of a symptomatic pseudocyst, and 1.3.22-1.3.23 give hereditary pancreatitis a 40% lifetime cancer risk with monitoring; the anaemia label omits that scan and pathway.

Inspiratory stridor in a 55-year-old with daily smoke exposure is an AAO-HNS 2018 expedited-laryngoscopy indicator and, at 45 and over, sits beside the NICE NG12 1.8.1 laryngeal cancer pathway; laryngitis does not cause stridor, so the larynx must be seen.

Headache, palpitations and light-headedness on regular stimulants plus decongestants is a sympathomimetic pattern closed by blood pressure and an office ECG; onset speed 3/10 is gradual so the Ottawa SAH rule is not triggered, and with no chest pain NICE CG95 1.2.1.3 does not apply.

Same sympathomimetic pattern as index 23 at age 50: blood pressure and an office ECG (higher yield for atrial fibrillation at this age) are the checks; gradual onset (3/10) and no chest pain mean no rule mandates imaging or troponin.

Inspiratory stridor as the sole complaint after a cold in a 30-year-old smoker with reflux: stridor is an AAO-HNS 2018 expedited-laryngoscopy indicator and is not a laryngitis symptom, so airway visualisation is mandated before the label stands.

Palpitations, light-headedness and breathlessness in a 31-year-old on four sympathomimetic exposures: the ESC 2018 initial syncope evaluation is an office ECG with vitals, PERC completes with pulse and saturation at age under 50, and no chest pain triggers NICE CG95.

New inspiratory stridor in a 104-year-old lifelong smoker is an AAO-HNS 2018 expedited-laryngoscopy indicator (stridor, tobacco history) with laryngeal cancer and aspiration on the differential; laryngitis does not explain stridor.

Coughing up blood in a 40-year-old smoker: NICE NG12 1.1.1 makes unexplained haemoptysis at 40 and over a suspected-cancer pathway referral and AFP 2015 makes a chest film the first test; viral pharyngitis does not explain it, and 9/10 submandibular pain in an immunosuppressed patient also needs abscess excluded (NG84 1.1.13).

Haemoptysis at 52 with slow-onset severe pharyngeal pain and no coryza or fever: NICE NG12 1.1.1 mandates a suspected-cancer pathway for unexplained haemoptysis at 40 and over and AFP 2015 a chest film; the viral label cannot explain blood.

Haemoptysis in an immunosuppressed 56-year-old: NICE NG12 1.1.1 suspected-cancer pathway for unexplained haemoptysis at 40 and over, and a chest film first (AFP 2015) with tuberculosis and pneumonia widened by immunosuppression.

Reported haemoptysis in an immunosuppressed smoker needs a chest film as the first test (AFP 2015) once nasal or pharyngeal bleeding is excluded; under 40 no NG12 pathway applies and the coryzal picture is benign, hence confidence 3.

Heavy menstrual bleeding with pallor and significant dyspnoea on a direct oral anticoagulant in a woman who may be pregnant is symptomatic blood loss: same-day haemoglobin, hCG and anticoagulant review are mandatory (a DOAC is contraindicated in pregnancy), and NICE NG126 1.4.5-1.4.7 routes a positive test with symptoms to an early pregnancy service; the anaemia label omits all of that.

Chest pain with significant dyspnoea and palpitations in a man with prior pericarditis: the 2015 ESC pericardial guideline makes ECG, troponin and echocardiography part of the diagnosis to exclude effusion and myopericarditis, which is beyond an office ECG.

Pleuritic positional chest pain with significant dyspnoea after a viral illness in a woman with prior pericarditis: ESC 2015 requires ECG, troponin and echocardiography before outpatient NSAID care, and dyspnoea is the symptom of effusion or myocardial involvement.

Significant dyspnoea with purulent sputum and wheeze in severe COPD with flare-ups is an exacerbation; NICE NG115 table 7 places severe breathlessness in the treat-in-hospital column and GOLD 2025 asks for pneumonia, heart failure and PE (5.9% in the PEP study) to be considered, so bronchitis is not an adequate basis.

All three cardinal exacerbation symptoms with significant dyspnoea in COPD with flare-ups in the past year: NICE NG115 table 7 makes severe breathlessness a hospital-assessment factor and the bronchitis label omits steroid and bronchodilator treatment; confidence 3 because COPD severity is not stated.

Significant dyspnoea in suspected SLE with prior pericarditis and a new hypertension consultation: ESC 2015 requires ECG and echocardiography for recurrent pericarditis with dyspnoea and EULAR 2023 requires same-visit screening for nephritis and serositis, so routine referral is not enough.

Malar rash, oral ulcers and arthralgia satisfy several EULAR/ACR 2019 domains, and significant dyspnoea with new hypertension points to serositis or lupus nephritis, which EULAR 2023 treats as organ-threatening: urinalysis, ECG and echocardiography are needed at this visit, not routine referral.

Significant dyspnoea and wheeze in severe COPD with flare-ups is an exacerbation that the anaemia label leaves untreated; NICE NG115 table 7 counts severe breathlessness toward hospital treatment and GOLD 2025 asks for pneumonia, heart failure and PE to be considered.

Significant dyspnoea and wheeze in a 59-year-old smoker with COPD is an exacerbation the anaemia label omits treatment for; NICE NG115 table 7 makes severe breathlessness a hospital-treatment factor and GOLD 2025 asks for pneumonia and PE to be considered.

Current chest pain with presyncope and palpitations at 55: NICE CG95 1.2.1.3-1.2.1.7 suspects ACS on associated symptoms regardless of sex and refers as an emergency while pain is present, and the HEART age band (45-64) needs troponin, not an office ECG alone, to reach low risk; panic and coronary disease coexist (Fleet 1996).

Chest pain with nausea and presyncope in a 47-year-old is a NICE CG95 1.2.1.3 ACS-suspicion combination with pain currently present (1.2.1.7 emergency referral), and the HEART age band requires troponin; the low pain score and panic features lower confidence to 3.

Fear of dying, choking, palpitations, derealisation and peri-oral tingling in a 27-year-old with chronic anxiety and no risk factors: HEART age scores 0, NICE CG113 1.3.6 asks only for the minimum investigations, and an office ECG with vitals closes the visit.

Mild non-radiating pain with palpitations and light-headedness in a 28-year-old with chronic anxiety: young age, female sex and atypical pain predict panic (Huffman 2003), the ESC 2018 initial evaluation is an office ECG with vitals, and no feature mandates troponin or imaging.

Sudden diffuse abdominal pain with the hyperventilation signature in a 27-year-old with chronic anxiety: abdominal examination, vitals and an office pregnancy test (NICE NG126 1.4.5-1.4.7 routes only a positive test with tenderness to an early pregnancy service) close the visit; bilateral, diffuse pain does not fit torsion.

Panic cluster (fear of dying, tingling, derealisation) in a 39-year-old with chronic anxiety and no cardiac risk factors: HEART age scores 0, and NICE CG113 1.3.6 minimum investigations (office ECG, vitals, abdominal examination) are the closing checks; near-syncope is why confidence is 3.

Textbook panic attack in a 32-year-old with chronic anxiety and depression: HEART age 0, NICE CG113 1.3.6 minimum investigations (office ECG, glucose, abdominal examination) close it; excess alcohol adds a withdrawal question but no mandated test.

Abrupt panic attack with sweating and tingling in an 18-year-old with chronic anxiety: pain is cramping and spreads to the abdomen rather than pleuritic and unilateral, so pneumothorax is excluded by chest examination and saturation (ordinary checks), and HEART age scores 0.

Unilateral 9/10 tonsillar pain with submandibular and laryngeal-level pain in a 56-year-old without coryza is the quinsy or supraglottitis pattern, but the deciding features (trismus, drooling, dysphagia, pain out of proportion to the pharynx) reach the intake only as a bare pain score; NICE NG84 1.1.13 referral turns on the examination.

Unilateral ear pain with cough after antibiotics for an ear infection is otitis media not yet settled; NICE NG91 1.1.14 refers only for mastoiditis, meningitis or facial palsy, none reported, so otoscopy and an antibiotic review close it.

Fever, sore throat, coryza, cough and myalgia after a sick contact is influenza-like illness; the poorly localised 8/10 headache lacks neck stiffness, rash or altered cognition, so NICE NG240 1.1.4-1.1.6 is checked by examination and the working diagnosis stands.

Inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting after a pertussis contact (Cornia 2010 likelihood ratios) mean probable pertussis rather than bronchitis; treatment is a macrolide and notification in the community, and no apnoea or breathlessness is reported.

Severe unilateral ear pain with coryza and cough on antibiotics is treatment-resistant otitis media; NICE NG91 1.1.14 hospital referral needs mastoiditis or intracranial signs, which are examination findings not reported, so an antibiotic change with review is adequate.

Gradual bilateral throat and tracheal burning with cough and hoarseness after a cold in a daycare worker is viral laryngopharyngitis; AAO-HNS 2018 reserves laryngoscopy for dysphonia past 4 weeks or a suspected serious cause, and no fever, dysphagia or stridor is reported.

Painful (7/10) swelling reaching both thighs in a man with a previously documented DVT scores at least 2 on the NICE NG158 table 1 Wells score (prior DVT, entire leg swollen, tenderness), which mandates a proximal leg-vein ultrasound within 4 hours; bilateral oedema with weight gain also needs heart-failure work-up that the localised-oedema label omits.

Bilateral ear pain with coryza on antibiotics at 68 is unsettled otitis media or eustachian dysfunction; NICE NG91 1.1.14 referral needs mastoiditis or intracranial signs, which examination checks, and diabetes was asked and is absent, lowering the malignant otitis externa concern.

Fever with unilateral ear pain on antibiotics in a 21-year-old is otitis media early in or failing treatment; NICE NG91 1.1.14 hospital referral needs a complication (mastoiditis, meningitis, facial palsy), none reported, so examination and an antibiotic review close it.

Fever, unilateral ear pain and cough on antibiotics for an ear infection is otitis media with a viral cough; NICE NG91 1.1.14 complications are examination findings not reported, and NICE NG120 treats the cough as self-limiting.

Bilateral symmetrical 8/10 sore throat with coryza in a 21-year-old fits viral pharyngitis; immunosuppression earns an immediate antibiotic and same-day blood count under NICE NG84 1.1.12 (high-risk tier) but without fever NG253 1.1.10 is not triggered, and no drooling, dysphagia or stridor mandates airway visualisation.

Fear of dying, derealisation, palpitations and tingling in a 24-year-old with chronic anxiety is a panic attack with HEART age 0; the pelvic pain and presyncope are closed by an office pregnancy test (NICE NG126 1.4.5-1.4.7 refers only a positive test with tenderness) and PERC completes with pulse and saturation.

Moderate bilateral sore throat with coryza after a sick contact is viral pharyngitis; immunosuppression without fever places him in the NICE NG84 1.1.12 high-risk tier (immediate antibiotic, blood count) but does not trigger NG253 1.1.10 or any airway rule.

Severe bilateral ear pain on antibiotics without fever or systemic features is unsettled otitis media or externa; NICE NG91 1.1.14 referral requires a complication found on examination, so otoscopy and an antibiotic change close it.

Bilateral ear pain with fever and cough on antibiotics is otitis media not yet responding, mislabelled as bronchitis but still benign; NICE NG91 1.1.9 advises review when symptoms persist past 3 days and 1.1.14 refers only for complications found on examination.

NICE NG79 1.1.9 lists severe frontal headache verbatim as a hospital-referral sign of intracranial complication, but the intake carries it only as a bare 8/10 score inside a slow-onset (0/10) coryzal febrile illness with no frontal swelling, meningism or neurology; the score alone cannot separate sinus pain from a complication.

Instantaneous mild (3/10) pain across both sides of the chest and abdomen with peri-oral and four-limb tingling and fear of dying is hyperventilation; pneumothorax pain is unilateral and pleuritic, so chest examination, saturation and peak flow (ordinary checks) close it and PERC completes with pulse and saturation at 21.

A groin lump that hurts on coughing and straining with preserved stool and gas and 2/10 pain is a reducible groin hernia; HerniaSurge 2018 names female sex and femoral site as incarceration risks, which sets the pace of elective referral, not an escalation.

Swelling extending into one thigh with 8/10 pain in a man on corticosteroids with heart failure and cirrhosis: NICE NG158 table 1 gives entire-leg swelling and tenderness 2 points, and even with the -2 for an alternative cause the pathway ends in a D-dimer or ultrasound, not an office check; the label also omits decompensation assessment.

Abdominal distension with no passage of stool or gas since symptoms increased (asked, absent) beside a groin lump in an obese 73-year-old woman is the obstructed femoral hernia pattern; HerniaSurge 2018 names female sex and femoral site as strangulation risks, and obstruction needs same-day surgical review and imaging, which 1/10 pain does not exclude.

Chest pain with significant breathlessness at 56 is a NICE CG95 1.2.1.3 ACS-suspicion combination with pain present (1.2.1.7), and the HEART age band needs troponin; purulent sputum with marked dyspnoea also needs pneumonia excluded by CRB-65 and a chest film, so bronchitis is not an adequate basis.

Mild (2/10), symmetrical, poorly localised swelling with weight gain in a 22-year-old with heart failure, nephrotic syndrome and a calcium-channel blocker is systemic oedema; on NICE NG158 table 1 the alternative diagnosis scores -2 and no tenderness is reported, and without dyspnoea the ESC 2021 congestion review is an outpatient adjustment.

Coughing up blood with fever needs a chest film as the first test (AFP 2015) before pharyngitis is accepted, and haemoptysis fails PERC; the coryzal sick-contact picture at 18 keeps the probability of pneumonia or PE low, hence confidence 3.

Fever while immunosuppressed: NICE NG253 1.1.10-1.1.11 says suspect neutropenic sepsis in people who become unwell on immunosuppressant treatment and refer immediately for secondary-care assessment; the viral features (cough, coryza, sick contact) do not lift that rule.

A raised groin lump that hurts on straining with 1/10 pain, preserved stool and gas and no distension is an uncomplicated hernia; HerniaSurge 2018 incarceration risks (female sex, femoral site, age 89) set a prompt elective referral, and no obstruction feature is present.

Bilateral slow-onset 3/10 swelling with heart failure, cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome is systemic oedema, but the one Wells point that would change the NICE NG158 pathway (deep-vein tenderness) reaches the intake only as a left calf site among five scattered pain sites; examination for asymmetry decides.

Unilateral eye and temple pain with lacrimation, congestion, a family history and alcohol trigger fits cluster headache, but the Ottawa SAH rule turns on whether a 7/10 onset score means peaking within an hour, and that time course reaches the intake only as a bare number; NICE CG150 1.3 makes first-bout cluster imaging a discussion, not a mandate.

Systemic oedema (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, calcium-channel blocker, NSAIDs) explains bilateral 3/10 swelling, but right calf pain with left thigh swelling is a scattered-site pattern, so the NICE NG158 tenderness point cannot be assigned from the intake and examination decides.

Slow-onset fever, chills, cough, coryza, myalgia and exhaustion is influenza-like illness; the NICE NG240 red-flag combination needs neck stiffness and altered cognition, and the pink raised painful lesions are not a non-blanching rash, so neck examination, a glass test and mental state (ordinary checks) close it.

Bilateral groin lumps worse on straining with slow onset, preserved stool and gas and no distension are inguinal hernias; the 7/10 pain and testicular ache are settled by reducibility and scrotal examination (HerniaSurge 2018 does not list male sex or pain as incarceration risks), so elective referral is adequate.

Fever in an immunosuppressed patient: NICE NG253 1.1.10-1.1.11 mandates suspecting neutropenic sepsis in people who become unwell on immunosuppressant treatment and immediate referral for secondary-care assessment, whatever the likely viral source.

A 10/10 violent periorbital headache involving both eyes with lacrimation fits cluster headache less well than index 229 (cluster is unilateral), and the Ottawa SAH rule depends on whether a 7/10 onset score means peaking within an hour; the time course reaches the intake only as a bare number, so the case cannot be decided.

Significant dyspnoea in COPD is a NICE NG115 table 7 hospital-treatment factor that the URTI label leaves untreated, and chest pain with breathlessness at 51 is a NICE CG95 1.2.1.3 ACS-suspicion combination needing ECG and troponin, not an office ECG alone.

Very slow-onset fever, sore throat, myalgia, sweats and exhaustion in a 55-year-old is influenza-like illness; the 4/10 headache with neck pain lacks stiffness, rash or altered cognition, so NICE NG240 1.1.4-1.1.6 is checked by examination and the working diagnosis stands.

Bilateral 9/10 violent forehead, cheek and eye pain without lacrimation in a woman on a vasodilator fits neither cluster headache nor the bronchitis label; the Ottawa SAH rule depends on whether a 7/10 onset score means peaking within an hour, which the intake gives only as a bare number.

Abdominal distension with no passage of stool or gas since symptoms increased (asked, absent) beside a groin lump and testicular pain is the obstructed inguinal hernia pattern needing same-day surgical review and imaging; 2/10 pain and no vomiting keep confidence at 3.

If the pericarditis label holds, fever and a subacute course are two major poor-prognosis predictors in the 2015 ESC pericardial guideline that mandate admission and echocardiography; if it does not, a subacute febrile illness with weight loss, nausea and flank pain needs same-day urine, bloods and a chest film, so outpatient pericarditis care is unsafe either way.

Significant dyspnoea with purulent sputum and wheeze in a 49-year-old smoker with COPD is an exacerbation that NICE NG115 table 7 counts toward hospital treatment, and bilateral chest pain with breathlessness is a NICE CG95 1.2.1.3 ACS-suspicion combination needing ECG and troponin.
